subject: 초기 국가의 창고 유적과 행정
title: Storehouses and the earliest administrations
content: Among the largest buildings dug up at many early sites are storehouses, and their remains tell us a good deal about how those ancient societies were run. A structure built to hold grain for a whole village implies that someone decided what went in and what came out, and the seals, tokens, and marked tablets found in such buildings record just those decisions. This makes the ancient storehouse the earliest archive we have. What the dug evidence shows is that these buildings appear before palaces and before temples of any size. In several ancient regions the order runs from shared storage to central storage to great architecture, which suggests that the power later shown in stone began by holding a surplus. The archaeology thus puts counting ahead of display in the growth of early states. Later periods make this picture busier without upsetting it. Once a civilization had scribes, the records they kept moved to their own buildings and the storehouse became one facility among many. Its early weight is still visible in the plans, and an archaeologist reading a site of that era treats the size and place of the storage rooms as evidence about how far the local power reached and how many households it drew on.

subject: 서아프리카 왕국의 도시와 학문
title: Cities and scholarship in medieval West Africa
content: Several large cities flourished in medieval West Africa, and the manuscripts saved from them have therefore changed how historians describe the region. Libraries built up over centuries held works on astronomy, law, medicine, and grammar, and many of them were copied locally because scholars there wanted their own copies. These collections show a written learned culture, whereas earlier accounts had assumed an oral one. Digging has confirmed how large the settlements were that carried this work. Excavated quarters show dense mudbrick building and mosques of real size, while survey of the land around reveals lesser sites that fed the centre. A medieval city of this kind needed farmland, a school, and a ruler willing to fund all of it, and the record keeps accounts of rulers who did exactly that. What later muddied this evidence was how frail the medium is. Manuscripts last only where they were kept dry and hidden, so the collections we hold are those that families chose to save through hard years, and their losses cannot be counted. Historians therefore treat the surviving libraries as one piece of what existed, although that piece alone is large enough to place these cities among the learned centres of the medieval world.

subject: 유럽의 삼림 고갈과 연료 전환
title: Woodland loss and the turn to coal
content: Pollen cores taken from bogs and lake beds record the woodland of medieval Europe thinning across several centuries, and the pattern is not uniform. Clearance advanced fastest around settlements and along rivers where timber could be floated, while remote uplands kept their trees far longer. Because these cores can be dated, historians read them alongside written records and find that the two agree about when particular districts ran short. What followed the shortage differed by region. Where woodland remained within reach, communities managed it by coppicing, cutting stems on a cycle so that the same stools regrown for generations, and the archaeological traces of this practice survive in hedgerows and old woods. Where no such reserve existed, households turned to peat or to coal outcrops, and the earliest coal working appears in exactly those districts rather than where the seams were richest. Scarcity therefore selected the technology rather than abundance doing so. The consequences reached beyond heating. Ironworking, glassmaking, and brewing all consumed fuel in quantity, and their locations shifted toward whatever remained available, so the map of medieval industry follows the map of fuel. Historians reading that correspondence treat woodland history as a constraint that shaped where things could be made at all.

subject: 중국 도자기 가마터가 말하는 기술 전수
title: What kiln sites reveal about passing on a craft
content: Excavated kiln sites in China preserve not only the vessels that succeeded but the far larger quantity that failed, and the wasters heaped beside a kiln are the most informative material a site can yield. Cracked bodies, slumped forms, and glazes that ran or blistered record the exact points at which a firing went wrong, and the sequence of such faults across the layers shows a workshop learning. This is evidence of instruction that no text describes. Kiln structures themselves changed in ways that can be dated. Longer chambers built up a slope drew air more strongly and reached higher temperatures, and the vessels fired in them are correspondingly harder and less porous. Where a new kiln form appears far from where it was developed, archaeologists ask whether the design travelled or whether potters did, and the answer often lies in the wasters, since a workshop that copied a form without understanding it fails in characteristic ways. What such sites establish is that technical knowledge in this craft passed through practice rather than through description. A potter learned by tending a firing beside someone who had tended many, and the archaeological record of failures is the only surviving trace of that apprenticeship.

subject: 중세 유럽 도시의 성벽과 확장
title: Medieval walls and the growth of towns
content: A medieval town wall was expensive to build and expensive to maintain, so its circuit was drawn tightly around what already existed rather than generously around what might come. When a town grew, the wall became an obstacle to its own inhabitants, and the archaeological record shows how repeatedly this problem arose. Excavations reveal suburbs spreading outside the gates, and later circuits enclosing them, sometimes three or four times across a few centuries. The successive lines can be dated from the masonry and from what lies beneath them. Each enclosure preserves the street plan of the moment it was built, so a modern city that grew this way carries a series of ring roads following walls that no longer stand. Where a circuit was never replaced, the town within it kept dividing its plots into narrower strips, and the resulting density is visible in the excavated foundations. What the walls also record is a judgment about danger. Districts that felt secure expanded without them, and the periods when new circuits were raised correspond to intervals of warfare in the written sources. Archaeologists therefore read wall construction as a dated response to threat, and its absence in a growing medieval town as evidence that the threat had receded.

subject: 자기기만은 어떻게 가능한가
title: How self-deception is possible
content: A person who deceives another knows the truth and conceals it, and this is straightforward enough. Self-deception seems to require the same person to occupy both roles at once, holding a belief while hiding it from herself, and stated that way the phenomenon looks impossible. Philosophy has therefore asked how something we observe constantly can be described without contradiction. One approach divides the mind, treating the deceiver and the deceived as distinct systems within a single person. This preserves the analogy with ordinary deception at the cost of a psychology many find implausible, since it posits an agent inside the agent who must itself be explained. Critics argue that the model solves the puzzle by restating it one level down. A second approach denies that self-deception involves holding contradictory beliefs at all. On this account a person manages her attention rather than her beliefs, avoiding the evidence that would settle the matter and dwelling on what supports the conclusion she prefers. Nothing contradictory is believed, and the deception lies in the motivated pattern of inquiry rather than in any state of mind. This account fits the evidence about how people actually maintain comfortable views, and it explains why self-deception is hardest to sustain when the disconfirming evidence cannot be avoided.

subject: 고대 그리스의 은광과 해군
title: Ancient silver mines and the fleet they built
content: The mines worked in ancient Attica have been dug in detail, and the galleries, washing tables, and cisterns cut into the rock therefore show an operation of real skill. Ore was crushed there and washed in channels that recycled scarce water, because the district had little of it, and the smelting furnaces left slag heaps that still cover those hillsides. The size of these heaps lets archaeologists judge how much the district yielded across the centuries it was worked. A famous episode in ancient history turns on this site. When an unusually rich vein was struck, the assembly of the city argued over whether to share the proceeds among its citizens or to build ships, and the choice to build therefore decided the war that followed. So the weight of a hillside in Attica rested on a political decision rather than on its geology alone. What the archaeology adds to the written account is the human cost. Bones and the size of the galleries show that much of this work was done by the enslaved in conditions that killed them quickly, whereas the ancient sources praising the fleet say almost nothing of it. Historians reading the two records together therefore treat these mines as a case where digging supplies what the literary tradition left out.

subject: 민주적 결정의 정당성
title: What makes a democratic decision legitimate
content: A majority vote settles a question, and yet the minority is bound by an outcome it argued against and may believe to be wrong. Political philosophy asks what makes such an imposition legitimate, and the answers divide according to whether they locate the value of the procedure in its results or in the procedure itself. Instrumental accounts hold that democratic decisions are legitimate because they tend to be better than the alternatives. Wider participation brings more information to bear, and rulers who must face an electorate attend to interests they would otherwise ignore. The difficulty is that this justification is contingent, since it would licence abandoning the procedure whenever some other method promised better outcomes, and few defenders accept that conclusion. Intrinsic accounts locate the value in equal treatment. Every citizen affected by a decision has an equal claim to a say in it, and a procedure that honours this claim treats people as it ought to whether or not the results are good. Critics reply that respecting persons cannot require imposing decisions that harm them, so results must matter somewhere. Most contemporary positions combine the two, holding that the procedure has independent value while remaining answerable to what it produces, and the interesting disputes concern how much weight each side carries.

subject: 기억과 개인의 서사적 정체성
title: Memory and the story a person tells
content: People understand their own lives as narratives, selecting episodes and arranging them so that later events follow from earlier ones, and some philosophers hold that this activity is what makes a person the individual she is. On this view identity is not a matter of continuous matter or of a persisting soul but of an ongoing account that the person composes and revises. The proposal explains a good deal that other theories leave obscure. It accounts for why we treat certain episodes as defining while forgetting most of what happened, and for why a person who repudiates her past seems to have become someone different in a sense that bodily continuity cannot capture. It also explains why moral repair often takes narrative form, since making amends involves retelling as much as compensating. Objections come from two directions. Some argue that many people simply do not experience their lives this way, and that making narrative essential to selfhood turns a cultural habit into a metaphysical requirement. Others observe that the stories people tell are demonstrably inaccurate, so grounding identity in them grounds it in fiction. Defenders answer that accuracy was never the point, since what the narrative provides is a shape within which deliberation and responsibility make sense.

subject: 초기 근대의 우편망과 정보 속도
title: Early modern posts and the speed of news
content: Before the telegraph, news travelled at the speed of a horse or a ship, and this simple fact shaped how far any authority could actually govern. Letters carried across early modern Europe took days or weeks depending on the season, and the delay was not merely an inconvenience, because a decision made in one capital rested on a picture of events that had already changed. Historians can measure these delays precisely, since surviving letters record both the date of writing and the date of receipt. What such measurements reveal is a landscape of uneven connection. Routes with relay stations moved letters several times faster than roads without them, so two towns at the same distance from a capital could stand weeks apart in effective terms. Maps drawn from postal records therefore show a geography quite unlike the physical one, and communities on a relay route belonged to a different world from neighbours a valley away. The consequences appear in how events unfolded. Rebellions succeeded or failed partly according to how quickly word reached those who might have intervened, and the historical accounts of such episodes make little sense until the delays are reconstructed. Historians accordingly treat the postal record as a necessary background to political narrative rather than as a separate technical subject.

subject: 감정은 판단인가 반응인가
title: Whether emotions are judgments
content: Fear seems to involve believing that something is dangerous, and anger seems to involve believing that one has been wronged, so philosophers have proposed that emotions simply are evaluative judgments of a certain kind. This account explains why emotions can be assessed as reasonable or unreasonable, and why arguing with someone can change how she feels. It places emotion within the space of reasons rather than outside it. The main objection comes from cases where the two come apart. A person who knows a spider is harmless may remain afraid of it, which means she holds the judgment and the emotion separately, and the emotion persists in the face of everything she believes. If emotions were judgments, such recalcitrance would be a contradiction rather than the ordinary experience it plainly is. Several repairs have been attempted. Some hold that the relevant state is a perception rather than a judgment, so that a thing can look dangerous while one believes it is not, exactly as a stick can look bent in water. Others treat emotions as composites in which a bodily response and an evaluation are combined. Both preserve the connection to reasons while allowing the two components to diverge, and the choice between them turns on how much weight the felt quality of emotion should carry.

subject: 중세 일본의 장원과 조세
title: Estates and obligation in medieval Japan
content: Land in medieval Japan was held under arrangements that no single term describes well, because an estate typically carried several overlapping claims rather than one owner. A cultivator worked a plot, a local manager collected from it, a distant proprietor received a share, and a shrine or temple often held a further entitlement, and each of these rights could be inherited or transferred separately from the others. Documents recording such transfers survive in large numbers. What these documents show is a structure that resembles a bundle of claims more than a hierarchy. Disputes accordingly turned on who held which right rather than on who owned the land, and the courts of the period developed detailed procedures for sorting them. Historians reading the archives find the same plot appearing in several collections held by different institutions, each preserving the portion of the record that mattered to it. The arrangement dissolved gradually as local warriors accumulated enough of the separate claims to act as sole holders. That consolidation is visible in the documents themselves, since the later ones record fewer parties and simpler terms. Historians therefore date the transformation of medieval Japanese landholding from changes in the paperwork rather than from any single event, and the process runs across generations rather than turning on a decree.
